title: Climate Zone Finder: Köppen Context for a Place
description: Identify a place's climate classification context with the Climate Zone Finder — Köppen groups explained with the thresholds that define them. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Los Angeles reads Csb — a dry-summer Mediterranean climate — while Miami is Am (tropical monsoon) and Chicago Dfa (hot-summer continental): three letters that compress thirty years of weather into a code.
quick_answer: The Climate Zone Finder identifies the climate classification context of a place — its Köppen climate group and what that code means in temperature and rainfall terms. Enter the place and read the zone, so planting, building and travel decisions start from the climate's actual character.

adds the winter-minimum detail gardeners actually plant by.
'Cfb' tells a mover more than 'mild': oceanic, rain spread through the year, summers rarely hot. Codes compress climate normals into comparable form.
Heating-dominated (D), cooling-dominated (A, B) or barely-either (C) — the group letter is the first energy conversation a design has with a site.
Köppen divided the world by the vegetation weather produces — thresholds students can test against any city's climate table, this finder's included.

C: temperate (coldest month between 0 and 18°C). s: dry summer. b: warm, not hot, summer. Los Angeles in three letters — and a gardener in Cape Town (also Csb) instantly knows the rhythm translates across hemispheres.
Phoenix is BWh: B (dry — rainfall below the temperature-dependent threshold), W (true desert), h (hot). Compare Tucson or Las Vegas — same family, same planning consequences for water.

popular_table.note: Second and third letters refine seasonality and summer heat (f = no dry season, s = dry summer, w = dry winter; a/b/c = hot/warm/cool summer). Borderline cities can sit within a degree or a few millimetres of a boundary — the code is a summary of normals, not a fence.

faq: Köppen (in its widely used Köppen–Geiger form): five letter groups defined by temperature and precipitation thresholds over 30-year climate normals. It is the world's standard climate taxonomy.

Classifications rest on standard 30-year normals (recent editions use late-20th/early-21st-century records). A specific dataset's vintage can nudge borderline places across a line — noted here rather than hidden.
My city feels hotter than its code.

Codes average decades and whole stations; urban heat islands run 1–3°C warmer than the classifying station in many cities. The code describes the region's climate; your street has its own microclimate.
Altitude creates Highland (H) microclimates inside any group — a Cfb valley can hold near-E conditions at its summits. Elevation tools on this site quantify the lapse that drives it.

A-group codes split into Af (rain all year), Am (monsoon — short dry season offset by heavy rains) and Aw (savanna — distinct dry winter). The second letter is where tropical places stop looking identical.
Does the finder give garden zones?
Köppen is climate science; USDA hardiness zones are the gardener's separate system, with its own finder on this site. Confusing the two is common and consequential for plants.
Oceanic versus continental — visible in the code?
Yes: Cfb (oceanic, mild winters, cool summers) versus Dfa (continental, harsh winters, hot summers) can share a latitude — London and Chicago sit near 51–42°N with utterly different codes.
